ety.text: From Middle English raven, reven (“raven (Corvus corax); carrion crow (Corvus corone); rook (Corvus frugilegus) (?); the constellation Corvus; gall nuts of the Aleppo oak (Quercus infectoria) used to make black ink”), from Old English hræfn (“raven”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrabn (“raven”), from Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz (“raven”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep- (“to crackle; to rattle”) or *ḱer- (“to croak, crow”), probably ultimately onomatopoeic, referring to the bird’s call.
A variant of ravin, from Middle English ravin, ravine, raven (noun).

senses.d: Any of several, generally large, species of birds in the genus Corvus with lustrous black plumage; especially the common raven (Corvus corax).
ex: [T]he Danes bare in their Enſigne a Raven vvrought (by report) in needle-vvorke, by the daughters of Lothbroke that is, Leather-breech, […]
Hee beareth Or, a Rauen Proper, by the name of Corbet.

senses.d: A jet-black, often glossy, colour, like that of the plumage of a raven (etymology 1, noun sense 1).
ex: Near-synonyms: ebony, onyx

senses.d: Usually preceded by a descriptive word: a bird from a genus other than Corvus that resembles the raven (etymology 1, noun sense 1), especially in having black plumage; also, an imaginary black bird.
ex: Along the wild mountains night-ravens were yelling— / They bodingly presaged destruction and woe.

senses.d: A flag bearing a raven (etymology 1, noun sense 1), formerly used by some Viking leaders
preceded by the: Viking military power.
ex: Behold the vvarrior bright vvith Daniſh ſpoils!— / The raven droops his vvings—and hark! the trumpet, / Exulting, ſpeaks the reſt.

senses.d: A person, especially a man, with black hair.
A person who brings bad news or makes pessimistic predictions.
Of the jet-black and often glossy colour of the plumage of a raven (etymology 1, noun sense 1).
ex: Near-synonyms: ebony, onyx
raven curls    raven darkness

senses.d: Sometimes followed by away or from: to obtain or seize (something, especially property) by force or violence; to plunder.
Sometimes followed by down, up, or (obsolete) in: to eat (something, such as food or prey) greedily; to devour, to wolf down.
ex: A Lion nevv returnde from rauening pray [prey], / came to the fount, his blood to vvaſh avvay.
Clusters of grapes, the which they raven'd quick / And roar'd for more; […]

senses.d: To absorb or take in (something, such as information) greedily; also, to approach or pounce on (someone) like prey.
ex: [S]he fenced them in their need / With iron-handed Duty's sternest creed, / 'Gainst Self's lean wolf that ravens word and deed.

senses.d: Followed by about, after, or for: to go after or seek for something, especially booty or spoils; to maraud, to plunder; also (generally), to move about wildly and cause damage; to rampage.
To eat greedily; also, followed by on or upon: of an animal: to prey on.
ex: The couaitous deſyre of riche men is euer vnſaciable. It always raueneth and neuer is ſatisfied.
And the hound Time, when all the Worlds and cities are swept away whereon he used to raven, having no more to devour, shall suddenly die.

senses.d: Sometimes followed by about or on: to move about searching for food or prey ravenously.
ex: [T]he Arms and Hands of the Bear, […] are his ſtrength and inſtrument of action to raven and prey vvith; […]

senses.d: Sometimes followed by after or for: to have a ravenous appetite or craving for food or prey.
ex: They passed along towards the great hall-door, where the winds howled and ravened for their prey; […]

senses.d: Originally followed by with: to experience great hunger; to be ravenous.
To take and exploit or make use of greedily.
Sometimes followed by after or for: to have a strong craving or desire for, or to do, something; to crave, to desire, to yearn.
ex: Here's my brother thirsting, ravening to make your acquaintance—and by George! you are in luck's way, young hopeful, to make his.

ety.text: From northern Middle English raven, from Old Norse ráfa (“to wander, roam”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Perhaps from a dissimilation of Proto-Germanic *wab(b)ōną (“to sway, waver, swing, shake, wobble, totter, reel, careen”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to move, swarm, waft”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk rava (“to wander, be delirious”). Doublet of rove.
English dialect raves, or rathes (“a frame laid on a wagon, for carrying hay, etc.”).

senses.d: An enthusiastic review (such as of a play).
ex: It was the critic's rave that made me want to see the show.

senses.d: A large-scale dance party with strobe lights and fast-paced electronic dance music, often illegally organized open-air or in underground venues.
ex: She has attended a rave every weekend this month.

senses.d: The genres of electronic dance music made to be played in rave parties.
ex: I danced to rave music all night.
Maybe I wear baggies / And white socks with flip-flops / Maybe I don't like listening to rave / And I'm not on the social mountaintops

senses.d: To be mentally unclear; to be delirious; to talk or act irrationally; to be wild, furious, or raging.
ex: Have I not cause to rave and beat my breast?
The mingled torrent of redcoats and tartans went raving down the valley to the gorge of Killiecrankie.

senses.d: To speak or write wildly or incoherently.
ex: "She is in trance. Your daughter, sir, is a powerful medium." "A medium! You are raving."

senses.d: To talk or otherwise express oneself with excessive enthusiasm, passion or excitement.
ex: He raved about her beauty.
The Lisbon mob, inflamed by the newspapers, and excited by the example of Brazil, raved a day or two for a republic

senses.d: To speak (a message) with intense enthusiasm, passion or excitement.
ex: She raved that she must seek revenge against the wrongdoers.
"Paloma, Paloma!" raved a delirious backer. "Paloma for a thousand!"

senses.d: To rush wildly or furiously.
ex:
Under a mightie rocke, gainst which do rave
The roaring billowes in their proud disdaine

senses.d: To attend a rave (dance party).
To wander or roam.
To stray or err.

ex: It was astonishing to see how he had gnawed the rave of the sled.
